What's Happening in Your Child's Brain
The Neurological Mechanism
The child's somatosensory cortex and proprioceptive system are under-responsive — they require more intense input to register sensation at baseline. When deprived of sufficient input, the brain generates a regulatory crisis. The basal ganglia, cerebellum, and brainstem collectively produce a drive to seek intense proprioceptive input: deep pressure, joint compression, impact.
Self-injury delivers exactly this input, activating Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles, triggering a rapid regulatory response. The behavior is automatically reinforced by its own sensory consequence: the nervous system is immediately calmer because the input need was met.
The Interoception-Regulation Loop: A poorly integrated interoceptive system means the child cannot identify dysregulation until the need becomes overwhelming — at which point, the fastest available pathway (self-injury) is engaged without conscious choice.
🧠 Parent Translation
Imagine being unable to feel your own hands unless you squeeze them as hard as you can. That's the closest analogy to what your child experiences. The hitting, the biting, the head-banging — they're not expressions of pain or anger. They're the brain's emergency regulation tool.
The hitting delivers deep pressure to joints and muscles. That pressure is a signal the nervous system desperately needs. When the need is met — even through self-injury — the child calms. This is why it's so hard to interrupt. It works.
Our job is not to take the tool away. Our job is to give the nervous system a better tool that works just as well — without the damage.

Self-injurious behavior most commonly emerges between ages 2–4, when proprioceptive and vestibular sensory needs are highest and the child has the fewest alternative communication and regulation tools. Without intervention, sensory-based SIB can consolidate into a deeply reinforced behavioral pattern.

Commonly co-occurs with: Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) | Attention Difficulties (ADHD) | Anxiety | Communication Delays | Intellectual Disability | Genetic Syndromes (Angelman, Fragile X, Rett Syndrome, Lesch-Nyhan)

The Technique: What It Is
Formal Name: Sensory-Based Self-Injury Replacement: 9-Material Protocol Parent-friendly alias: "Meeting the Need Safely"
Sensory-based self-injury occurs when a child's nervous system uses physically harmful behavior — head-banging, self-biting, hitting, scratching, hair-pulling — to obtain the intense proprioceptive, vestibular, oral-motor, or tactile input it requires for regulation. Unlike self-injury driven by communication, sensory-based SIB is automatically reinforced: the behavior itself produces the sensory consequence the nervous system needs.
This protocol introduces 9 categories of therapeutic materials that deliver equivalent or superior sensory input through safe, non-injurious pathways — meeting the nervous system's regulatory need without causing physical harm. The child is not learning to "stop" the seeking; they are learning to seek through a safer channel.
Domain
Sensory Processing / Behavioral Safety / Nervous System Regulation
Frequency
Daily sensory diet; reactive use during high-need moments. Ongoing integration throughout daily routine.
Age Range
2–12 years. Technique Code: D-409
Discipline Lead
Primary: Pediatric OT. Co-Lead: ABA/BCBA. Supporting: NeuroDev Medicine, SLP, Special Education.
Who Uses This Technique
This technique crosses therapy boundaries — because the nervous system doesn't organize by therapy type.
🟠 Occupational Therapy — Primary Lead
OTs conduct sensory processing assessments (Sensory Profile, SPM) to identify the specific type and intensity of sensory input the child is seeking. OTs design the individualized sensory diet, select appropriate materials, and teach implementation. For sensory-based SIB, OT is the cornerstone discipline.
🔵 ABA / BCBA — Co-Lead
BCBAs conduct functional behavior assessments (FBA) to confirm the SIB is sensorily maintained versus attention, escape, or tangible functions. This distinction is critical — sensory materials won't reduce non-sensory SIB. ABAs also design the replacement behavior training that teaches the child to access materials independently.
🟢 NeuroDev Pediatrician
NeuroDev physicians rule out pain-related SIB (ear infection, dental pain), provide diagnostic clarity, and — in severe cases — support pharmacological intervention as an adjunct to sensory strategies.
🟣 Speech-Language Pathology
For children with self-biting or oral-seeking self-injury, SLPs manage the oral-motor component: selecting appropriate chewy tools, calibrating resistance levels, and integrating oral-motor alternatives into the broader program.
What This Protocol Targets
PRIMARY: Reduce Self-Injurious Behavior
Decreased frequency of head-banging, self-biting, hitting, scratching, hair-pulling. Reduced intensity of episodes. Shorter duration of individual SIB events. Decreased tissue damage.
SECONDARY: Proprioceptive Regulation
The child's nervous system learns to achieve regulation through safer sensory channels. Observable: child reaches for sensory tool when dysregulated; longer intervals between SIB episodes when sensory diet is in place.
SECONDARY: Interoceptive Awareness
Improved ability to detect internal states before crisis. Observable: child shows early warning signals before SIB escalation; responds to parental redirection at lower arousal levels.
TERTIARY: Emotional Regulation + Participation
Reduced overall frequency of meltdowns and dysregulation episodes. Ability to participate in daily routines, school, and social activities without escalation to SIB. Reduction in caregiver anxiety and injury management burden.
Meta-analysis (World J Clin Cases, 2024): Sensory integration therapy promoted adaptive behavior, participation, and regulation across 24 studies. → PMC10955541
Materials 1–3 of 9
The 9 Materials: Weighted, Oral-Motor & Crash
Nine material categories. Each targets a specific sensory input the child's SIB is seeking. Match the material to the topography — what the child does tells you what input they need.
Material 1 — Weighted & Compression Gear
Seeking signal: Head-banging, whole-body pressing, hitting self Sensory mechanism: Sustained deep proprioceptive input — the same "heavy" feedback that impact delivers, provided continuously and safely.
  • Weighted blankets (≤10% body weight)
  • Weighted vests | Compression vests/shirts
  • Weighted lap pads | Body socks

Seeking signal: Self-biting of hands, arms, skin Sensory mechanism: Intense oral-motor proprioception — jaw muscles working against resistance, same feedback as biting without tissue damage.

  • Chewable jewelry | ARK Therapeutic chewies

Material 7 — Tactile Seeking Tools
Seeking signal: Scratching self, skin-picking, pinching Sensory mechanism: High-intensity tactile stimulation that competes with self-injury's sensory feedback — hands need an equally intense safe target.

Material 8 — Sensory Diet Tools
Seeking signal: Chronic, recurrent SIB (the need builds throughout day) Sensory mechanism: Proactive scheduled input prevents the regulatory crisis that triggers SIB — fill the sensory tank before it runs empty.
  • Visual schedule boards | Countdown timers
  • Sensory break cards
  • Portable sensory kit for outings
Price range: ₹0–2,000 🛒 Search on Amazon.in: visual schedule board children therapy
Material 9 — Calming Environment Tools
Seeking signal: SIB triggered by sensory overload (too much input → seeking intense input to override chaos) Sensory mechanism: Environmental input reduction prevents the overload trigger — the environment itself becomes preventive intervention.
  • Noise-canceling headphones | Dimmable lamps
  • Pop-up tent/canopy (calm corner) | Sound machine
  • Organized storage

Safety First: Before You Begin
Self-injurious behavior requires a safety-first approach. Read every item below before implementing any strategy.
🔴 RED — DO NOT PROCEED without professional assessment if:
  • SIB is causing significant tissue damage, open wounds, bruising, or injury requiring medical treatment
  • Child is engaging in eye-pressing, eye-poking, or visual-related SIB (specialized OT required immediately)
  • Head-banging is severe, forceful, or raising concern for concussion or head injury
  • SIB has escalated rapidly in frequency or intensity (rule out pain-related trigger: ear infection, dental pain, GI discomfort)
  • The function of the behavior has NOT been confirmed as sensory through professional assessment
  • Child has significant medical complexity or genetic syndrome
🟡 AMBER — MODIFY and proceed with caution if:
  • Child is currently in a dysregulated state (wait for window of calm)
  • Child is unwell, feverish, or showing signs of physical discomfort
  • You are alone with the child and cannot safely manage acute escalation
  • Child has not previously encountered the material (introduce gradually, one material at a time)
🟢 GREEN — Safe to proceed when:
  • Functional assessment has confirmed sensory function (even informally)
  • Child is in a baseline-regulated state
  • Materials have been inspected for safety (chewy items for wear/cracks; weighted items for safe weight)
  • You are prepared to accept the behavior without punishment or physical restraint

STOP IMMEDIATELY if: Child shows severe escalation of SIB → sudden onset of new SIB topography → signs of physical injury requiring medical attention → acute medical distress during session. 🆘 For urgent guidance: FREE National Autism Helpline 9100 181 181 (24x7, 16+ languages)
Set Up Your Space
The right environment is the first intervention. Set up before the child enters the space.
Room Layout Essentials
[1] CRASH CORNER — Mattresses stacked, away from walls
[2] CALM TENT — Dim, enclosed, soft floor
[CENTER SPACE] — Clear floor, no furniture hazards
[3] MATERIAL STATION — Weighted vest, chewy, tactile tools — all within child's reach at their height
[4] PARENT POSITION — 2 meters from child, visible but not hovering
[5] DATA TALLY — Paper on wall for immediate recording
Setup Checklist
  • All SIB-risk surfaces padded or removed (sharp corners, hard walls near known SIB zones)
  • Sensory materials accessible to child independently — within arm's reach at their height
  • Crash surface in place BEFORE the session begins
  • Chewy tool cleaned, inspected, and within child's sight
  • Lighting dimmed or softened (avoid fluorescent overhead)
  • Noise sources identified and reduced (TV off, phone on silent)
  • Visual schedule showing current session is visible to child
  • Parent/caregiver is in calm emotional state (child's nervous system reads yours)

You are not controlling the child. You are controlling the variables. The environment tells the nervous system whether it is safe or threatened.

Step 1 of 6
⏱️ 30–60 seconds
Step 1: The Invitation
Principle: Every session begins with an invitation, never a command. The child's nervous system must feel safe before it can accept new input.
"I have something for you. Want to see?" [Hold up the chewy / weighted item / tactile ball — whichever matches today's need] "You can hold it / wear it / squeeze it. Let's try."
Parent Body Language
  • Crouch to child's eye level
  • Open body posture — no crossed arms
  • Calm, low voice — even if you're anxious
  • Offer the item without forcing contact
✅ Acceptance Cues (green light)
  • Child reaches for item or leans toward it
  • Child makes visual contact with the material
  • Body posture softens (even slightly)
  • Any vocal/gestural acknowledgment
⚠️ Resistance Cues (modify or postpone)
  • Child turns away or pushes item away
  • Arousal level increases at the introduction
  • Immediate SIB escalation upon approach

ABA Pairing Principle: Before introducing the material as a functional replacement, the child must associate it with positive experiences. If this is a new material, the first 3–5 sessions are purely about pairing. Replacement training comes after the material has positive value.
Step 2 of 6
⏱️ 1–3 minutes
Step 2: The Engagement
Principle: The child is now in contact with the material. Deepen the interaction by allowing the child to explore at their own pace — guided by you, never forced.
For Chewy Tools
"This is for biting. You can bite it hard. As hard as you want." Model biting motion. Allow child to bite with full intensity. Do not correct the force.
For Weighted Vest/Blanket
"This is a heavy hug. Can I put the heavy hug on you?" Apply slowly. Watch for acceptance signals. If tolerated for 5 seconds — that is success in early sessions.
For Crash Pad
"Let's crash! Ready? Jump!" Model the crash yourself first. Make it fun, not clinical.
For Tactile Tools
"Squeeze this as hard as you can." Hand child the highest-resistance item. Allow intense manipulation.
Engagement Indicators
  • ✅ Child continues engaging with material for any duration
  • ✅ Child appears to reduce arousal during engagement
  • ✅ Child initiates re-engagement after brief pause
  • ⚠️ Child tolerates but shows no affect change — continue, pairing is still building
  • ❌ Child completely disengages — do not force; end session; try different material tomorrow

Reinforcement Cue: The moment the child engages: "Yes! Good! You're doing it!" — immediate, specific, enthusiastic. Within 3 seconds.
Step 3 of 6
⏱️ 3–10 minutes
Step 3: The Therapeutic Action
Principle: This is the active therapeutic event — the point at which the child's nervous system is receiving the input it seeks through the safe alternative. Duration and intensity are more important than perfection.
Weighted/Compression → Full-Body Proprioceptive Saturation
Child wears compression vest or is wrapped in weighted blanket. The input is continuous and passive. Target: 15–20 minutes of wear. Not continuous all day — 20-minute blocks every 60–90 minutes.
Chewy Tube → Sustained Oral-Motor Work
Child bites chewy with intensity and duration they choose. Do not limit force. Do not redirect to "gentle biting." The jaw needs to work hard. Allow 3–5 minutes of intense chewing. The chewy should show indentations — that means it's working.
Crash Pad → Impact Seeking Protocol
Allow and encourage full-body impact — jumping, crashing, rolling. The landing must be felt. Target: 10–15 crash cycles or until the child shows regulatory shift (reduced agitation, slower breathing).
Heavy Work → Resistance Through Effort
Assign a heavy work task: carrying weighted bag room to room, pushing a box, pulling resistance band, pushing against a wall for 10 counts. Rotate through 3–4 activities. Total: 5–10 minutes.
Vibration Tool → Targeted Proprioceptive Input
Apply vibration to the specific body areas the child typically targets in self-injury. Arms, back, shoulders. Allow child to hold tool and apply themselves. Target: 2–3 minutes per body region.

Red Line During Execution: If SIB occurs during the session — do NOT stop the session punitively. Calmly redirect to the alternative: "Here. Bite this." or "Here. Crash here." — within 3 seconds of SIB.
Step 4 of 6
⏱️ 3–5 minutes
Step 4: Repeat & Vary
Therapeutic Dosage Principle: 3 high-quality, fully engaged repetitions are worth more than 10 forced repetitions through a disengaged child. Read the nervous system's satiation point.
Material

Variation Options (within same session or across days):
  • Crash pad: Vary approach (jumping vs. running vs. rolling into it)
  • Heavy work: Change activity type (carrying → pushing → pulling)
  • Chewy: Offer different texture/firmness level on alternating days
  • Weighted: Vest during morning routine vs. blanket during quiet time
  • Tactile: Cycle between spiky ball → putty → textured disc

Do not continue past satiation — the nervous system has received what it needed. Continuing past the child's satiation point can create negative associations with the session.
Step 5 of 6
⏱️ Within 3 seconds
Step 5: Reinforce & Celebrate
Core ABA Principle: Timing matters more than magnitude. Immediate, specific, enthusiastic reinforcement within 3 seconds of the target behavior increases the probability of the child using the safer alternative again — and again — until it becomes the default.
What to Reinforce
  • ✅ ANY contact with the safe alternative material (even brief)
  • ✅ Self-initiation of reaching for material (highest priority — reinforce intensely)
  • ✅ Tolerating wearing/holding material for any duration
  • ✅ Completing 1 crash cycle, 30 seconds of chewing, or any duration of heavy work
  • ✅ Redirecting from SIB to alternative when prompted (even if partially)
The Reinforcement Script
"YES! You used the chewy/vest/crash pad! That was amazing!"
Pair with child's preferred reinforcer from their reinforcement menu. Celebrate the attempt, not just the success.
Every child needs an individualized reinforcement menu — their most powerful motivators. These may be: preferred toys, screen time tokens, food items, social praise, physical play, or sensory items themselves.
🛒 Reinforcement Menu Tool — ₹364 | ₹589
Step 6 of 6
⏱️ 2–3 minutes
Step 6: The Cool-Down
Principle: No session ends abruptly. The nervous system needs a transition signal — a predictable bridge from high-input therapeutic engagement back to baseline.
Transition Warning (2 min before end)
"Two more times, then all done." Show visual timer if child uses visual supports.
Reduce Intensity Gradually
From crash pad, transition to weighted blanket sitting. Lower voice and movement cues — the parent's calm nervous system models regulation.
Material Put-Away Ritual
"Let's put the chewy away. Your turn." Child participates in storage if able. Offer a comfort item or next activity visual.
Post-Transition Rest
Move child to a preferred, low-demand activity. Never immediately into a high-demand situation. The nervous system needs 5–10 minutes to consolidate the regulatory gain from the session.

If Child Resists Ending: Offer choice: "Two more crashes, then done — or one more crash and then [preferred item]?" Never physically remove the child from the material against resistance — this creates negative associations. Give 30-second extended time, then use firm, warm, consistent transition cue.

What If It Didn't Go As Planned?
Most sessions have friction. This is not failure — it is feedback. Here are the 7 most common challenges and their immediate solutions.
Problem 1: Child refuses all materials immediately
Why: Materials are unfamiliar; no pairing has occurred; current arousal too high. Fix: Back up to pairing only — offer material with zero demands for 3–5 sessions before attempting replacement. Never introduce new materials during acute SIB.
Problem 2: Materials don't seem to reduce SIB frequency
Why: Either the material's intensity is insufficient, or the function is not purely sensory. Fix: Increase intensity — heavier weight, firmer chewy, more intense crash. Or request formal functional assessment from BCBA to confirm function.
Problem 3: Child uses materials briefly then returns to SIB
Why: Material is in early stages; SIB still "wins" the sensory competition. Fix: This is actually progress — brief material contact means it's competing. Increase reinforcement intensity. Increase material intensity. Continue consistently.
Problem 4: SIB escalates during session
Why: Arousal too high at start; session demands are overwhelming. Fix: Stop structured session. Move to passive heavy input (weighted blanket, dim room). No demands. No talking. Let the nervous system settle.
Problem 5: Child becomes dependent on constant material access
Why: Expected and appropriate — the child has found something that meets the need safely. Fix: This is the goal. Consistent access IS the intervention. Begin gradually shaping independence across time.
Problem 6: Other caregivers don't use materials consistently
Why: Lack of training; skepticism; logistics. Fix: Use the Share This With Your Family resources. Caregiver inconsistency is one of the biggest barriers to SIB reduction.
Problem 7: Protective gear is working but SIB hasn't decreased
Why: Protective gear reduces harm but doesn't replace the sensory input — SIB is still meeting the need. Fix: Gear is harm reduction, not treatment. Ensure active sensory alternatives are running in parallel.
"Session abandonment is not failure — it is data."
Adapt & Personalize
No two nervous systems are identical. Your child's sensory profile determines which variations work best.
Under-Responsive Child (Input Seeker — SIB from understimulation)
Needs MORE intense input. Lean toward: crash pad, heavy work, firm chewy, vibration. Sensory diet should be input-dense throughout the day. Calm environments may actually increase SIB risk — monitor closely.
Over-Responsive Child (Input Seeker from Overwhelm — SIB from chaos)
Needs REDUCED input chaos first, then controlled proprioceptive input. Lean toward: calming environment first, then weighted compression in quiet space. Avoid loud, busy settings during material introduction.

Parent applies materials (no independent use yet). Short durations (1–3 min). High-frequency brief inputs. Heavy adult guidance.
5–7 years
Teach independent access with visual cues. "When you want to bite, get your chewy." Practice during calm times.
8–12 years
Collaborative selection of materials. Child participates in sensory diet planning. Socially appropriate portable options (discreet chewy, pocket fidget).
Topography-Specific Customization:
  • Head-banging → Crash pad + weighted vest are PRIMARY
  • Self-biting → Chewy tube is PRIMARY; supplemented by oral-motor diet
  • Hitting/slapping self → Heavy work + vibration are PRIMARY
  • Scratching/skin-picking → Tactile tools (spiky ball, putty) are PRIMARY
  • Hair-pulling → Compression hood/weighted headband; fidget tools in hands
Progress — 15%
Weeks 1–2
Week 1–2: What to Expect
The first two weeks are not about behavior change. They are about nervous system introduction. Your child is encountering new sensory pathways. The goal is: any contact, any tolerance, any moment of regulation through a safer alternative.
What You May See
What It Means
Child tolerates weighted vest for 5–10 seconds
Proprioceptive pathway is responding — this is real progress
Child picks up chewy and holds it (even without biting)
Association with the material is forming
SIB frequency is unchanged but intensity may vary
Normal in weeks 1–2; substitution takes time to establish
Child shows brief calm after crash pad engagement
The input IS working, even if the effect is short-lived
You feel frustrated or doubtful
Expected; the 8-week arc is long; this is the hardest phase

What is NOT expected yet: Spontaneous self-initiation of materials | Significant decrease in SIB frequency | Generalization to new settings | Independent regulation. Week 1–2 asks you to celebrate 3-second material contacts. That is the right level.
Progress — 40%
Weeks 3–4
Week 3–4: Consolidation Signs
Something shifts between weeks 3 and 4. The child begins to anticipate the materials. They may reach for the chewy before biting their arm. They may move toward the crash pad when arousal rises. These are not accidents — these are the early signs of neural pathway consolidation.
Behavioral Change
Neural Pathway Significance
Child approaches material station unprompted
Alternative pathway is being voluntarily accessed
SIB begins but stops sooner when material is offered
Competition between pathways — the material is gaining value
Child carries chewy or holds weighted item during transitions
The nervous system is proactively seeking the safer input
You notice longer intervals between SIB episodes
Sensory diet is preventing regulatory crises
Child shows recognizable "seeking look" before approaching material
Emerging interoceptive awareness

When to Increase Frequency/Intensity: If consolidation indicators appear: ✅ Add one more sensory diet input slot per day | ✅ Increase crash pad session duration by 5 minutes | ✅ Begin practicing independent material access with reduced adult prompting.
Parent Milestone: You may notice you are more confident. You are reading your child's nervous system signals earlier. You are offering the material before the SIB escalates. This is the parent-as-therapist arc beginning to function.
Progress — 75%
Weeks 5–8
Week 5–8: Mastery Indicators
🏆 Mastery Criteria for D-409: The child has moved from passively tolerating sensory alternatives to actively using them as their primary regulation tool — across multiple settings and topographies.
✅ Self-Initiation
Child independently reaches for designated material when dysregulation is rising — without adult prompt — in ≥3 out of 5 observable opportunities.
✅ Competition
SIB episodes have decreased in frequency by ≥30% from baseline week data. Individual SIB episodes, when they occur, are shorter.
✅ Generalization
Child uses materials in at least 2 settings (home + school, or home + car).
✅ Parent Confidence
Caregiver can implement the sensory diet independently without reference to protocol.

Mastery Unlocked → What Comes Next: Maintain current sensory diet | Begin reducing protective gear as material use solidifies | Add proactive communication training: teach child to request sensory input verbally or via AAC | Begin D-410: Building Sensory Diets for High-Risk Children.
Celebrate This Win
To Every Parent Who Has Made It to This Card:
You started here: watching your child hurt themselves and feeling completely helpless. You stood in the gap between the child's need and the harm it was causing, and you refused to accept that nothing could be done.
You learned the science — that your child's nervous system wasn't broken, it was seeking. You gathered the materials. You set up the space. You ran the sessions on hard days, when you doubted, when the data didn't show change yet.
And now, somewhere in the past 5–8 weeks, your child reached for the chewy instead of their arm. Or landed on the crash pad instead of the wall. Or wore the vest and sat through something that would have triggered SIB six weeks ago.
That is not a small thing. That is neural pathway change. That is the result of your work.

Journal Prompt: "Eight weeks ago, the most frequent challenge was ________. Today, I saw ________. The difference is ________." Family Celebration Suggestion: Document this milestone. Take a photo of your child using their sensory tool. Write down the first time they self-initiated. These moments are the evidence that what you did mattered.
Share your milestone with our parent community: pinnacleblooms.org/community | WhatsApp: 9100 181 181
Red Flags: When to Pause
Even with progress, these signs mean pause and seek professional guidance immediately.
🚨 IMMEDIATE MEDICAL ATTENTION:
  • Any SIB episode causing head injury, significant bleeding, or wounds requiring medical treatment
  • Eye-related SIB (pressing, poking) with any change in vision
  • Loss of consciousness, confusion, or neurological symptoms following head-banging
  • Sudden escalation of SIB to an intensity or frequency that cannot be safely managed
🔴 CLINICAL CONSULTATION URGENTLY (within days):
  • SIB has not decreased at all after 4+ weeks of consistent implementation (function may not be sensory)
  • New SIB topography appearing (child who banged head now also biting)
  • SIB escalating in intensity despite sensory alternatives being in place
  • Signs of pain associated with SIB onset (holding ear, touching teeth, guarding abdomen)
🟡 TELECONSULT RECOMMENDED (within 2 weeks):
  • Uncertainty about sensory diet design or material selection
  • Child accepting materials but SIB not responding after 3–4 weeks
  • Caregiver burnout affecting implementation consistency
  • School reporting SIB patterns that differ from home patterns

Escalation Pathway: Minor concern → Call FREE Helpline 9100 181 181 Clinical concern → Book teleconsultation at pinnacleblooms.org Medical urgency → Emergency medical care immediately "Trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, pause and ask."

Path B — SIB reduced but environment still triggering:
→ D-411: Environmental Modifications for Sensory Safety — Redesigning home, school, and community environments to prevent SIB triggers.
Path C — Alternatives established, communication gap remains:
→ B-Series Communication Techniques — Teaching verbal or AAC-based requests for sensory input, replacing body-to-body communication with words/symbols.

Long-term developmental goal: A child who can independently identify their sensory state, request appropriate input verbally or through AAC, and access regulated states through self-managed tools — without SIB.

Families Who've Been Here
These are not marketing stories. These are clinical narratives from Pinnacle Blooms Network® families — with behavioral specificity that reflects what this journey actually looks like.
Chennai, Age 6 — Head-Banging
Before: Arjun banged his head against walls and floors up to 40 times per day. He had bruising above his right temple. His family had padded every wall in their home. His mother had not slept through the night in 18 months.
Turning point: OT assessment revealed intense proprioceptive under-responsiveness. Crash pad, weighted vest, and heavy work schedule introduced.
After (8 weeks): Arjun began running to the crash pad when arousal rose. Head-banging dropped to 3–5 times per day by week 6. By week 10, his teacher reported 80% reduction in classroom SIB.
"The wall padding is still there. But now it's for jumping into the crash pad. Not for his head."
Hyderabad, Age 4 — Self-Biting
Before: Meera bit her own hands and forearms until they bled. Her parents had tried mittens, restraint, and saying "no" for 14 months. Nothing worked. The wounds were infected twice.
Turning point: Chewy tube introduced with intensive pairing across 10 sessions. A firm chewy necklace worn throughout the day. Oral-motor heavy work added to all meals.
After (6 weeks): Meera began reaching for the chewy necklace when the biting urge arose. By week 12, her arms had healed completely.
"The mouth needed to bite. We gave it something to bite. That's the entirety of the logic — and it works."
Bengaluru, Age 9 — Head-Hitting and Scratching
Before: Rahul hit the sides of his head with both fists during transitions and scratched himself when under-stimulated. School had flagged it as "behavioral" and applied consequences. The consequences made it worse.
Turning point: FBA confirmed sensory function. Heavy work protocol before every transition. Spiky tactile ball always in his pocket.
After (10 weeks): Rahul was doing "wall push-ups before class" as his own pre-transition ritual. Head-hitting reduced by >70%. School re-classified his plan as sensory support.

Frequently Asked Questions
Q1: Is it safe to let my child bite hard on the chewy or use the crash pad with full force?
Yes — this is the entire point. The chewy is designed to withstand intense biting without breaking. The crash pad is designed to absorb full-body impact. These materials are therapeutically calibrated to be safe at the exact intensity your child needs. Trying to limit the intensity defeats the purpose — the nervous system needs intense input, and mild alternatives won't compete with self-injury.
Q2: My child won't touch any of the materials. What do I do?
Back up to pairing before any functional use. Introduce each material as a play object with zero demands for 5–10 sessions. Let the child explore it in their own time. Materials that have been forced on children rarely become voluntary tools. Pairing takes time — it is worth the investment.
Q3: How do I know if the SIB is truly sensory and not attention-seeking?
Sensory-maintained SIB occurs when the child is alone, across settings without a consistent social trigger, and produces an observable calming effect. If SIB is primarily in front of caregivers and decreases when attention is available, request a formal FBA from a BCBA before proceeding with sensory materials alone.
Q4: How long do I need to run the sensory diet?
A sensory diet for a child with significant SIB is not a time-limited intervention — it is a regulatory support system, like glasses for a child with poor vision. Plan for long-term maintenance with periodic OT reassessment.
Q5: Is protective gear like a helmet a failure?
No. Protective gear is a legitimate, clinically appropriate harm reduction tool during the transition period. Using protective gear while building safer alternatives simultaneously is responsible clinical management.
Q6: My child uses the chewy all the time now. Is that okay?
Yes — this is success. A child with a chewy in their mouth throughout the day is meeting their oral sensory need safely. Do not restrict chewy access as a consequence for behavior — this removes the tool that is working.
Q7: Should I stop the self-injury when it happens?
Do not physically restrain the behavior without immediately providing an alternative. The protocol is: offer the safe alternative within 3 seconds of SIB onset, using a calm prompt — "Here. Bite this / crash here / squeeze this." Physical restraint alone increases distress and often escalates SIB.
Q8: Where do I get professional help if I can't afford private OT?
Call 9100 181 181 — Pinnacle's FREE National Autism Helpline (24x7, 16+ languages). Our clinical coordinators can connect you with government therapy resources, low-cost OT options, and parent-level training to maximize what you can do at home.
